title: Custom site or a page builder
metaTitle: Custom code or a page builder
excerpt: Use a page builder when the team will edit often and the layout fits the tool. Use custom code when the interaction, the speed, or the ownership cannot.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table, weighing whether that layout can live in a builder.
caption: A layout on a laptop, still small enough to accept or refuse. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When is a page builder the right tool for a company site?
faqs.answer: Use one when the pages are marketing pages, the layout fits the tool's sections, and non-engineers will edit them often. Accept that an unusual interaction may need to be simplified. If you cannot name a behavior the builder cannot do, you are probably not ready to leave it.

faqs.question: When should a site be custom code instead?
faqs.answer: Move to custom code when a real interaction has to match the product, when you cannot meet a speed bar because the tool's runtime is in the way, or when you cannot own the project and the accounts. A preference for a particular stack is not, by itself, the reason.

faqs.question: What speed numbers are worth naming in the decision?
faqs.answer: Google's Core Web Vitals thresholds are a clear bar: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. Measure the real page on a phone, with the real images. A demo made of gray boxes is not the test.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
The decision in custom website vs webflow is about who will edit the site, and whether the layout can live inside a builder. Choose a builder when the team will change the pages often and the design fits the tool's sections. Choose custom code when the interaction, the speed, or the ownership cannot be honest inside those limits.

Both can look polished on a sales call. The difference shows up the month you need a page the template did not imagine, or a result you can measure.

## When a builder is the right home

A page builder is a good home when the site is a set of marketing pages, the people who change the words are not engineers, and the layout is a sequence of sections you can name in advance. A founder who will rewrite the headline twice a month should not wait on a pull request for that sentence.

Use a builder when these are true:

- The pages are marketing: home, offer, about, a few landing pages, a contact path.
- The interactions are the ones the tool already does well: links, simple forms, a menu, a content collection.
- Two or three people in the company will edit, and they will actually do it.
- You accept that a very custom interaction may be simplified to fit the tool.

That is a real product, not a compromise to be ashamed of. Many early companies need a clear site this month more than they need a codebase. Webflow, and tools like it, exist so a small team can publish without staffing a front-end role. If that is your situation, stay. Do not commission a custom build to satisfy a stack preference.

The limit is the sentence you just accepted. You are agreeing that the tool's section model is the design system. If your pages are mostly those sections, you will move faster in the builder than in a repository nobody wants to open.

## When the layout hits the wall

The wall is specific. You need a layout the builder cannot hold without a pile of embeds, custom code blocks, and exceptions nobody can edit. A pricing page with a simple toggle is usually fine. A configurator, a logged-in view, or a page that has to match a product interface pixel for pixel is often the wall.

Watch for these signs during the design, before you have built yourself into the tool:

- The designer is drawing states the builder will flatten into one frame.
- The content model needs relationships the collection cannot express, so people start pasting the same sentence in twelve places.
- Someone proposes an embed for the one part that matters, and the embed will not match the type, the color, or the mobile behavior.
- The editor preview and the live site disagree, and the team has started "just checking production."

At that point, more time inside the tool is how the exception becomes the site. Move the part that does not fit, or move the site. A hybrid can work: the marketing pages stay in the builder, and one custom tool lives on its own URL. Pretending one tool does both, with hidden code in every page, usually fails the editor and the engineer at once.

Hanabi's production sites are built in Next.js, React, and TypeScript, styled with Tailwind, with motion in the Motion library when the page needs it. That stack is the custom side of this choice. It is the right side when the page has to behave like a product. It is unnecessary machinery when the page is a letter with a few sections.

## Speed you can measure

Speed is a reason to leave a builder only when you have a target and the tool cannot meet it for the page you actually need. Taste is not a measurement. Core Web Vitals are.

[Google's Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) are the numbers to hold: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. Those are the thresholds Google publishes for a good experience, and they are the ones worth naming in a build. A builder that meets them on a simple marketing page is fine. A builder that misses them because every section loads its own behavior, and you cannot remove that behavior, is a reason to move the page into code you can control.

Measure the page you will ship, on a phone, with the images you will use. A demo with gray boxes is not the test. If the hero is a large photograph, that photograph is the test. Marketing assets should be sized for the slot, not dropped in at camera resolution because the editor allowed it.

Custom code does not grant the numbers by existing. A Next.js site on Vercel can still ship an oversized image and a layout that jumps. The advantage is that you can fix the cause: the image, the font, the shift. In a builder, the cause is sometimes the runtime you are not allowed to touch. That is the ownership problem hiding inside the speed problem.

## Ownership

Ownership means you can leave. You can export the content, you understand where the pages live, and a new person can edit them without a specialist who has vanished. Ask this before you sign, for either path.

In a builder, ownership is the project file, the CMS collections, the domain, and the billing account in the company's name. If the agency owns the workspace, you do not own the site. Put the transfer in the scope. Confirm you can edit after the engagement without a monthly permission you did not mean to buy.

In custom code, ownership is the repository, the hosting account, the environment variables, and a README a new engineer can follow. A repository you cannot run is a folder of files. Hosting on Vercel, or anywhere else, should be the company's account. The same is true of the database if the site has one. Prisma and PostgreSQL are ordinary tools for that kind of site. They are also a responsibility: backups, migrations, and a person who can apply them.

Content is the part people forget. A builder often makes content easier and code harder to take with you. A codebase often makes the code yours and the editing path something you must design on purpose. Decide which loss you can accept. If the founders will edit every week, design the editing path first and pick the tool that makes those edits safe.

## Interaction that has to be real

Some interactions are decorative and can be cut. Some are the product. A menu that opens, a form that validates, a page that responds to a choice: those should work on a phone, with a keyboard, and without a wait that makes the person click twice.

If the interaction is a prototype of the software you sell, build it in the same language as the product when you can. A marketing page that simulates the product in a builder, beside a product built in React, will drift. The day the product changes, the simulation lies. Founders feel this as "the site looks old," when the real problem is two sources of truth.

Motion belongs in this test. A small transition that makes a panel feel connected is worth keeping when it does not block the first read. A sequence that plays for six seconds before the offer appears is a tax. In code, you can tie that motion to a reduced-motion setting and keep the page usable. If the builder makes the sequence mandatory, the sequence is a reason to simplify or to move.

Do not choose custom code because you want the site to "feel expensive." Choose it because a specific behavior has to be true: a comparison that matches the product, a page that stays stable while images load, an editor your engineers will use. If you cannot name the behavior, you are not at the wall yet. Stay in the builder until you can name it.

## Decide before the rebuild

Write the decision on one page.

1. Who edits the site in a normal month, and which tasks they do.
2. The interactions that must match the product, if any.
3. The speed bar: the three Core Web Vitals thresholds, checked on the real page.
4. Whose accounts the site lives in, and how you leave.

If the first line is "the founder edits copy" and the second line is empty, use a builder. If the second line has a real interaction, or the accounts cannot be yours in the builder, use code. If you are unsure, design the page in Figma first and see whether every frame maps to a section the tool already has. The frames that do not map are the scope of a custom build.

Rebuilding later is allowed. It is cheaper when the content is structured and the domain is yours. It is expensive when the site is a pile of absolute positions and the only person who can publish is a contractor. Choose the path you can operate, then hold it until the wall is real.

The builder question often narrows to one tool. Framer is the one many teams mean when they say they want to design the marketing site in the browser. Whether that should become the production home, or stay a design tool beside a codebase, is the next decision: [Framer or a production codebase](/blog/framer-or-a-production-codebase).

If you want that choice made against your actual pages, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
